report:
The evidence strongly contradicts the premise that this claim is false. Abaloparatide does reduce vertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

**Findings:**

- **Pivotal RCT (ACTIVE trial):** The phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled ACTIVE trial (n=~2,463 postmenopausal women) found new vertebral fracture incidence of 0.58% with abaloparatide vs. 4.22% with placebo at 18 months (p<0.0001) — an 86% relative risk reduction. Nonvertebral fractures were also reduced by ~43% ([JAMA, 2016](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640)).

- **FDA approval basis:** Based on ACTIVE and ACTIVExtend data, the FDA approved abaloparatide (Tymlos) specifically for reducing vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk. The FDA label itself cites the 86% relative risk reduction ([FDA label, TYMLOS](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/208743s017lbl.pdf)).

- **Extension study (ACTIVExtend):** Continued follow-up with sequential alendronate therapy maintained fracture-risk reduction, with a 87% relative risk reduction in vertebral fractures sustained at 25 months versus placebo-then-alendronate ([PMC7112966](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7112966/)).

- **Network meta-analysis:** An independent meta-analysis confirmed abaloparatide reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk versus placebo and compares favorably with other osteoporosis therapies ([Osteoporosis International, 2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-019-04947-2)).

**Conclusion:** The claim is well-supported by high-quality randomized controlled trial data, FDA-approved labeling, extension studies, and independent meta-analyses. It is **true**, not false — abaloparatide significantly and consistently reduces vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. You may want to revisit whatever source led you to doubt this claim, as it conflicts with the weight of clinical evidence.
